problem: The function ${y}_{1}(t)={t}^{3}$ is a solution to the equation ${t}^{2}{y}^{″}-3t{y}^{′}+3y=0$ for $t>0.$ If ${y}_{2}=u(t){y}_{1}(t)$ is a second solution of the equation, then which of the following equations must be satisfied by $u(t)?$

feedback.problem: The function ${y}_{1}(x)={e}^{-4x}$ is a solution to the equation ${y}^{″}+8{y}^{′}+16y=0.$ If ${y}_{2}=u(x){y}_{1}(x)$ is a second solution of the equation, then which of the following equations must be satisfied by $u(x)?$
feedback.worked_solution:
We're given that

$$
{y}_{2}(x)=u(x){y}_{1}(x)=u{e}^{-4x}.
$$

Differentiating ${y}_{2}=u{e}^{-4x}$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′} & ={u}^{′}{e}^{-4x}-4u{e}^{-4x} \\ {y}_{2}^{″} & ={u}^{″}{e}^{-4x}-8{u}^{′}{e}^{-4x}+16u{e}^{-4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({u}^{″}{e}^{-4x}-8{u}^{′}{e}^{-4x}+16u{e}^{-4x})+8({u}^{′}{e}^{-4x}-4u{e}^{-4x})+16u{e}^{-4x} & =0 \\ {u}^{″}{e}^{-4x} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${e}^{-4x}\ne 0$ for all $x,$ we must have

$$
{u}^{″}=0.
$$
